prompt: Which of these statements about twisted-pair Ethernet cabling are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The receiver measures the voltage difference between the two wires of a pair, so interference that affects both wires equally cancels out
options.explanation: Correct in the ideal differential model. Twisting and cable balance help common-mode rejection; real receivers reject interference only to the extent their balance and performance allow.

options.text: Common four-pair building-cabling Ethernet standards support 100 m channels with the required category and installation quality
options.explanation: Correct for those specified PHYs/channels, not every Ethernet variant or transceiver.

options.text: Every copper cable propagates signals faster than every optical fibre, guaranteeing lower end-to-end latency
options.explanation: False. Velocity depends on construction and optical wavelength; some copper cables are faster than ordinary glass and others slower. PHY processing also contributes to latency.

options.text: The signal travels at the speed the electrons move through the wire
options.explanation: The signal is a guided electromagnetic wave; drift velocity is a different quantity depending on the current and conductor.

workedExample:
Ideal common-mode cancellation:

```formula
(V_1 + n) − (V_2 + n) = V_1 − V_2
where
V_1: the signal voltage on the first wire of the pair, in volts
V_2: the signal voltage on the second wire, in volts
n: the noise voltage picked up equally by both wires, in volts
In words: noise that reaches both wires equally disappears when the receiver subtracts one wire's voltage from the other's.
```

Real rejection is finite. The specified common Ethernet channels support 100 m when all requirements are met. Propagation speed must be read from the cable/fibre specification, and complete latency includes electronics. Electron drift is not the signal speed.

prompt: You carry a laptop from next to a Wi-Fi access point to a room 25 m away through two walls. Throughput falls from 600 Mbit/s to 60 Mbit/s. Which are plausible contributing mechanisms, requiring measurements to confirm? Select all that apply.

options.text: Received signal strength falls with distance and wall absorption, so SNR drops
options.explanation: Plausible. Distance, obstacles and multipath can reduce received signal and SNR; the exact indoor loss is not determined by a free-space formula alone.

options.text: With lower SNR, the radios switch to modulation with fewer bits per symbol (for example from 1024-QAM down to 16-QAM)
options.explanation: Plausible. Rate adaptation may choose a more robust modulation/coding scheme; it does not necessarily choose the densest constellation from SNR alone.

options.text: More frames are corrupted and must be retransmitted at the link layer
options.explanation: Plausible. More unsuccessful attempts can consume airtime. A retransmission can deliver previously lost data; goodput counts each useful byte once and includes the cost of failed attempts.

options.text: Propagation delay over 25 m slows each frame down
options.explanation: 25 m at nearly c is about 83 nanoseconds. That's negligible against frame times of tens to hundreds of microseconds; distance hurts through signal strength, not travel time.

workedExample: Weaker signal, a lower selected PHY rate and extra retries are plausible mechanisms. The extra 25 m propagation is only about 83 ns and cannot explain the stated tenfold throughput drop. Measure signal/noise, PHY rate, retries, contention and backhaul before diagnosing or choosing a fix; a mesh node is not a guaranteed remedy.
